# Appendix B. Co-design and the SovTech vision {#sec-appendix-codesign}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## This appendix is not part of the course
The modules teach running the tool and defending the analysis. This appendix covers the project behind the tool: why Q-CRAFT Explorer was built, and what it is a proof of concept for. Nothing in the capstone depends on this appendix. Read it to influence what the next version does.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## This is not an IMF product
Q-CRAFT Explorer, this course and everything proposed below are an independent project by [Teal Insights](https://tealinsights.com) and [NatureFinance](https://naturefinance.net). None of it is an official IMF product and none of it carries IMF endorsement. The work is meant to be complementary to the IMF's own training materials and to the Q-CRAFT User Guide [(Tim and Rahman, 2024)](references.qmd#src-user-guide), which remain the authoritative references. Nothing in this appendix should be read as a criticism of a tool the IMF Fiscal Affairs Department built for its own technical assistance and made available to everyone.
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**What you need to know:**

- Q-CRAFT is a proof of concept for a larger goal: making the LIC-DSF more usable through human-centered design
- The biggest barrier to using fiscal projection tools well is ergonomics
- We are looking for co-design partners, not endorsements
:::

## Ergonomics is the biggest barrier to using fiscal projection tools

**Across this class of tools, design stops people who can handle the economics.** The tools do not guide them through the decisions they must make. The observation is general and predates this project. It is not a claim about the Q-CRAFT workbook, whose brief [Module 5](m5-boundaries.qmd) sets out.

Years of conversations with MoF economists, central bank staff, and IFI economists all pointed the same way. So we ran structured design sprints and discussions with practitioners who use these tools daily.

## We rebuilt Q-CRAFT as a web app and verified it against the Excel workbook

**[Q-CRAFT Explorer](https://teal-insights.github.io/QCraft-App/explorer/) reimplements the IMF's Q-CRAFT Excel workbook as an open-source web application.** The [calculation engine](https://github.com/Teal-Insights/QCraft-App/tree/main/packages/qcraft-engine) is a Python reference package, developed and tested separately from the interface, with automated parity tests against the original Excel tool. The Explorer runs a TypeScript port of it, checked against the Python engine on the same runs.

The testing pipeline is public and automated. Baseline parity is exact for 147 of 147 tested countries: zero percentage-point deviation across debt-to-GDP, revenue, primary balance and primary expenditure as shares of GDP, with a further 25 parameter sensitivity combinations passing. Climate-scenario parity is confirmed for ratio metrics only, meaning debt-to-GDP, revenue and expenditure as percent of GDP. Higher-stakes tools need the same transparent, automated verification. [Module 1](m1-how-qcraft-thinks.qmd) has the fuller statement of what the parity claim covers.

The deployed app carries that verification into the workflow and ships two data modes. Current, the default, bundles the latest WEO and UN population releases. Verified uses the workbook's own vintages, so any number can be checked against the original. Source-record context panels sit beside ten of the twelve controls, showing what the underlying sources publish while you choose. Any control moved off its Explorer default gets a CHANGED badge and a one-line rationale field, and the export annex records all twelve settings either way. Three teaching widgets are linked from the header. The export packet contains the charts, the CSVs, the assumptions annex and a run file that restores the whole configuration, in one download. Because the app builds to a static bundle, a ministry can serve it inside its own network with one command, no outside connection required.

## Q-CRAFT is the proof of concept

Q-CRAFT is deliberately small: ten user-facing controls, one core equation.

**The real goal is the LIC-DSF, the Low-Income Country Debt Sustainability Framework.** It is far more complex, far more consequential, and used for every low-income country. We already work with LIC-DSF end-users and want to work with its designers too.

```{mermaid}

    style E fill:#1ABC9C,stroke:#2C3E50,color:#fff
```

Each front-end serves a different need:

1. Web Explorer (current). Select a country, choose the assumptions with the source records beside you, compare scenarios, export the packet.
2. Guided Analysis Tool (planned). AI-assisted help deciding what to enter and why. Always available, cheaper than a technical assistance mission.
3. DSF Integration (the goal). Q-CRAFT and [DIGNAD](glossary.qmd#gloss-dignad) feeding into LIC-DSF assumptions through the same ergonomic layer.

**Today, if you do not know what to enter for a parameter, you go looking for guidance away from the screen where the choice has to be made.** The context panels and rationale field are the first pass at design that makes the right thing easy and the wrong thing hard.

## The co-design invitation

**The current version is live, and practitioner input shapes the next one in five areas.**

1. Parameter guidance. What would make the six context panels more useful, and what heuristics do experienced practitioners use that the panels do not carry?
2. Default assumptions. What are sensible defaults by country type? Should defaults vary by region?
3. Capacity development integration. How would this tool fit into an actual CD workshop or IMF mission?
4. Validation priorities. Which countries and scenarios should we prioritize for verification?
5. Missing features. What is the first thing you would want that is not here?

We are asking for a few hours from a few people: design feedback, a continuing conversation as we build, and word on whether we are making something useful.

We are not asking for official endorsement, confidential information, or money: we understand institutional constraints and work with publicly available materials. Everything is permissively licensed open source, free to use, copy and improve.

## Q-CRAFT delivers value now and proves the approach

**We start with Q-CRAFT for two reasons:**

1. Immediate value. A co-designed Q-CRAFT tool could be in use within weeks, costs nothing, and requires minimal commitment to evaluate. It complements, not replaces, the Excel workbook.
2. Pioneer the approach. We prove the design process works on a small tool before applying it to the LIC-DSF.

## The SovTech vision

Central banks have been applying technology to supervisory functions for years. The BIS documented "SupTech generations", a framework for technology in supervision and regulation [(di Castri et al., 2019)](references.qmd#src-dicastri-2019). The open question is when sovereign debt management will catch up.

**We call this SovTech: SupTech principles applied to sovereign debt analysis.** Three principles guide this work:

Modularity respects how people work. Components fit together like building blocks, so a team can swap one module without rebuilding everything.

Open source makes the tool institutional infrastructure. Anyone can examine how the analysis is done, and the permissive MIT license puts no barrier to adoption.

AI has made analytical software dramatically cheaper to build, and a trust layer makes it safe to rely on. Sovereign debt analysis serves policy decisions worth billions of dollars. At those stakes, verification pipelines, automated testing, and human-in-the-loop governance are requirements. Hence the parity verification pipeline described in [Module 1](m1-how-qcraft-thinks.qmd).

Q-CRAFT Explorer is our attempt to show what this looks like. The source code is on [GitHub](https://github.com/Teal-Insights/QCraft-App). We welcome your input.
